message.content:
The first time Jesus is mentioned in a non‑Christian historical source is in the writings of the Jewish historian **Flavius Josephus**.  
In *Antiquities of the Jews* (book 18, chapter 3, section 3), written around 93–94 CE, Josephus refers to “James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ.”  The passage is widely accepted by scholars as containing a genuine core reference to Jesus, though it has been subject to later Christian interpolation.

A few decades later, the Roman historian **Tacitus** mentions Jesus in *Annals* (book 15, chapter 44, section 2) written around 116 CE.  Tacitus records that “Christus” (the Latinized form of Christ) was executed by Pontius Pilate during the reign of Tiberius.

These two references are the earliest surviving mentions of Jesus in the historical record outside the New Testament.  The earliest Christian text that mentions Jesus is the Gospel of Mark, written sometime between 70 CE and 80 CE, but it is part of the Christian canon rather than an independent historical source.
